**Location:** McGill University, Montreal  
**Scientists:** Ernest Rutherford & Robert B. Owens  

- Rutherford and Owens observe that **thorium oxide continuously emits a radioactive gas** that remains radioactive for several minutes.  
- They name this gas **"emanation"** (from Latin *emanare*, to flow out).  
- This is the **first observation of radon** (as thorium emanation, or "Th Em").  
- **Color:** 🔵 (Rutherford & Owens)  

> 💡 *Note: This was the fifth radioactive element discovered (after uranium, thorium, radium, polonium).*

---

## 📌 1899 – Radium Emanation Observed  
**Scientist:** Friedrich Ernst Dorn (Germany)  

- Dorn observes that **radium compounds emit a radioactive gas**.  
- He names it **"radium emanation" ("Ra Em")**.  
- He independently confirms the existence of a distinct radioactive gas from radium.  
- **Color:** 🟡 (Dorn)  

> 💡 *This gas is later identified as 222Rn (the most stable isotope of radon).*

---

## 📌 1900 – Actinium Emanation Discovered  
**Scientist:** André-Louis Debierne (France)  

- Debierne observes that **actinium compounds emit a radioactive gas**.  
- He names it **"actinium emanation" ("Ac Em")**.  
- This leads to the recognition of **three distinct emanations**:  
  - Radon (Ra Em)  
  - Thoron (Th Em)  
  - Actinon (Ac Em)  
- **Color:** 🟢 (Debierne)  

> 💡 *Each emanation was thought to be a separate element at the time.*

---

## 📌 1909 – Isolation of "Radium Emanation"  
**Scientists:** Sir William Ramsay & Robert Whytlaw-Gray  

- Ramsay and Whytlaw-Gray **isolate and purify "radium emanation"** from radium salts.  
- They conduct detailed experiments to determine its physical and chemical properties.  
- They **propose that the emanation may be a new noble gas**, similar to helium, neon, or argon.  
- This is a pivotal step in classifying radon as a noble gas.  
- **Color:** 🔴 (Ramsay & Whytlaw-Gray)  

> 💡 *They believe the gas is a member of the noble gas family due to its inertness and low reactivity.*

## 📌 1911 – Acceptance as a Noble Gas  
**Body:** International Commission for Atomic Weights  

- The International Commission for Atomic Weights **officially accepts "radium emanation" as a new element**.  
- It is recognized as a **noble gas**, part of a new group in the periodic table.  
- This marks the **first formal recognition of radon as a distinct element**.

- Some analyses argue that **elevated risk only occurs at high indoor concentrations (>100 Bq/m³)**.
